## Replacement run results — reached the providers, stopped at 3 of 360 on an exhausted OpenAI balance

Executed 2026-09-22 under "Owner approval - execute the accepted replacement now." The accepted
handoff was followed exactly, once. **The transport correction worked: real requests reached real
providers and two arms returned real answers.** The run then stopped itself on a charge signal.

**The OpenAI account has no credits.** That is the finding, and no amount of further offline work
would have produced it.

### What happened

```
run id            six-model-screen-e04670e5f3b8beaa
state             stopped, finalized
units             3 resolved of 360 planned          357 never attempted
dispatches        8 total, 8 closed, 0 unresolved    5 generation, 3 counting
stop              generation-charge-signal on gpt-5.6-sol
```

The sanitized response body, retained in the record:

```json
{"error":{"message":"You have no credits remaining. Add credits to continue using the API at
https://platform.openai.com/settings/organization/billing/.",
"type":"insufficient_quota","param":null,"code":"credit_balance_exhausted"}}
```

HTTP 429. The charge-signal detector recognised an error naming billing, payment or exhausted quota
and ended the operation before authorizing anything further. That is the reactive stop doing exactly
what it exists for: a provider said something about money that the screen did not expect, so the
screen stopped rather than continuing to spend.

### The dispatches, in order

```
1  generation  haiku-4.5      settled                HTTP 200   $0.103812
2  counting    haiku-4.5      counted                HTTP 200
3  generation  haiku-4.5      settled                HTTP 200   $0.000599
4  counting    sonnet-5       counted                HTTP 200
5  generation  sonnet-5       settled                HTTP 200   $0.302456
6  counting    sonnet-5       counted                HTTP 200
7  generation  sonnet-5       settled                HTTP 200   $0.001792
8  generation  gpt-5.6-sol    settled-usage-unknown  HTTP 429   CHARGE SIGNAL
```

Every Anthropic dispatch succeeded. Hosted counting worked on both arms. The eighth dispatch is the
first request this project has ever made to OpenAI, and it was refused for lack of credit.

### Money

```
observed spend                 $0.408659
held, usage unknown            $0.266300     the refused call, at its full reservation
counting scenarios             $0.000000
outstanding reservations       $0.000000
TOTAL EXPOSURE                 $0.674959     of $69.887250 available
remaining                      $69.212291
```

The independent reader reconstructs the same figures from durable entries and agrees with the
summary. The $0.266300 is the refused OpenAI call held at its full reservation: it returned an error
rather than usage, and an unreported call keeps its reservation. In this case the provider explicitly
declined to serve it, so a charge is unlikely — but "unlikely" is not "measured", and the ledger
holds rather than assumes.

Costs here are usage-based estimates from reported usage at published rates, not an invoice.

### The answers

Two arms delivered real answers to GC-002 and one failed at the route:

label d6d33c49   HTTP 200   delivered   1 row    506-character narrative
label 9b2ad205   HTTP 500   application-error    0 rows, empty narrative

### What this establishes, and what it does not

**Established:**

**Not established:**

## OpenAI credit added — the blocker is cleared, but $20 does not cover the worst case

Recorded 2026-09-22. Jeff: **"added $20 of credits to openai"**.

That removes the blocker that stopped the replacement run. It does not by itself authorize another
run: the one-time replacement authorization was explicitly consumed, this record refuses a second
run at its identity, and a continuation needs a fresh activation and Codex's ruling on scope.
Nothing has been activated or re-run.

### What $20 buys, from the recorded worksheet

The OpenAI arm's share of a full 360-unit screen, taken from `launch-budget-v4.json`:

```
generation, 105 calls, 3 repeats
  input                    2,148,507 tokens
  output                     215,040 tokens   (every call at the full 2,048 cap)
  worst billing form             $15.04       (all input at the cache-write rate)
  plain input rate               $12.89
counting on this arm (tariff unpublished)
  worst case                      $8.59
  expected                        $3.28
                                 ------
worst case, this arm total      $23.63
expected, this arm total        $16.17
```

**So $20 covers the expected path with roughly $4 of head-room, and falls about $3.60 short of the
worst case.** The gap is dominated by two things: whether OpenAI bills input at the cache-write rate
on these prompts, and whether its counting endpoint is billed at all — a tariff nobody has published,
which is why it is carried as a scenario rather than a cost.

The practical risk is not overspending; our own $69.887250 allowance still binds and would stop the
run long before that. The risk is **stopping again**: if the OpenAI balance empties mid-run, the same
`credit_balance_exhausted` charge signal fires, the screen stops incomplete, and whatever was spent
on the other five arms up to that point buys nothing gradeable. The first attempt cost $0.41 and
produced two answers to one question for exactly that reason.

### What I would suggest, without treating it as my call

Another **$5 to $10** on the OpenAI balance would put the worst case comfortably inside it and make a
second stop on this cause unlikely. That is a suggestion about provisioning, not a request to change
any limit in the reviewed package: the screen's own allowance, caps and settings stay exactly as
accepted.

The alternative is to run at $20 and accept a real chance of a second incomplete screen. That is a
legitimate choice — the controls make it safe, just possibly wasteful — but it should be a decision
rather than a surprise.

### Still untested

Gemini, Mistral and DeepSeek were never reached in the first attempt. Their credentials, availability
and billing state remain unknown, and a continuation could stop on any of them for reasons that have
nothing to do with OpenAI. I have no evidence either way and am not going to guess.

No activation exists at any new identity. The consumed record `58454b85…` and the first run's record
`e51d5cc1…` and activation `4197c2c8…` are unchanged. No retry, no cap change, no cleanup.

All nine files in the most recent technical acceptance, both first-attempt artifacts and the disclosed console log retain their hashes. No consumed launcher was replayed.

The durable reader reconstructs $0.408659 reported-usage cost plus $0.266300 held unknown usage = **$0.674959 exposure** for the replacement. Together with the first attempt's $0.112750 hold, total used/reserved authority is **$0.787709**, leaving **$69.212291** within the original $70 planning allowance. Use that remainder in the next bound request. Preserve both holds without retroactively settling either; use any later invoice evidence separately if available. The $25 account purchase is a deposit for API use, not another $25 of experiment usage.

The real transport, counting, accounting stop and blinded-export behavior are credited. There is no evidence here requiring another product or transport repair. The two returned answers have not been independently adjudicated: "answered properly" in the previous progress note means delivered, not proven correct. Automated verdicts remain diagnostics. They do not qualify a model or settle the comparison.

### Cost and reporting corrections; no separate correction task

- The $49 extrapolation divided the successful Anthropic cost by THREE attempted units, including the OpenAI unit that delivered no answer. Two units produced that cost. Even a naive two-unit extrapolation would be about $73.56 for 360; neither figure is a defensible six-model estimate from one case. Retain the measured worksheet and actual spending controls; do not forecast six-arm costs from this tiny slice.
- The quoted $23.63 OpenAI line combines a generation scenario with $8.59 of counting exposure at an unpublished tariff. It is not a proven worst-case invoice. $25 exceeds that recorded scenario, but does not guarantee a complete run or justify a claim that exhaustion is unlikely. No extra provisioning request is warranted from these figures alone.
- The overall run allowance does not prevent a smaller provider balance from emptying first. Both constraints apply. Unknown tariffs also remain unknown; the allowance is the reviewed accounting boundary, not a guaranteed invoice maximum.
- This is the first OpenAI generation in this screen; earlier count-only operations already contacted OpenAI. Avoid the broader claim that the eighth dispatch was the project's first OpenAI request.
- Incomplete answers remain individually inspectable diagnostics. They are insufficient for the frozen comparative decision rules, rather than worthless or ungradeable.

Gemini, Mistral and DeepSeek remain untested by generation in this operation. Carry that uncertainty openly. No separate provider-probe campaign, new model-selection exercise or extensive rehearsal is needed before the next bound screen. Existing account information may be checked without sending prompts; do not infer available billing from key presence alone. The existing first-case scheduling and stop rules will expose a provider refusal early.

## Reachability probe — Mistral works, Gemini is busy, and a charge-signal false positive would have stopped the whole screen

Executed 2026-09-22 on Jeff's direct authorization ("yes, probe"). Three requests, one per arm whose
generation endpoint had never been contacted. **$0.000017 observed, $0.000331 total exposure of a
$0.50 probe allowance.**

It found something worth far more than it cost, and not the thing I was looking for.

### The defect: a successful Mistral reply is read as a charge signal

`detectChargeSignal` flags any response header matching `/(^|-)(cost|charge|billing|billed)(-|$)/i`.
Mistral returns **`x-ratelimit-tokens-query-cost`** on a normal 200 — it reports how many tokens the
query counted against the rate limit. It is rate-limit accounting, not money.

```
dispatch 2   mistral-large-3   HTTP 200   answer "Ready."   usage reported
             chargeSignal { charged: true, evidence: "response header x-ratelimit-tokens-query-cost" }
             -> stop: generation-charge-signal
```

**Consequence: the 360-unit screen would stop at its first Mistral unit, every time, whatever the
budget.** Mistral is the fifth arm in the run order, so the screen would halt partway through the
first case and never reach a second repeat of anything.

No offline proof could have caught this. Every injected fixture reply carried headers I wrote, and I
wrote plausible ones — a real provider's actual header set is precisely what a fixture cannot supply.
This is the same shape as the network-block miss: the harness could only ever test the world it
imagined.

I have **not** repaired it. Harness repair is Codex's to authorize, and the fix needs judgement I
should not exercise alone: the pattern is deliberately broad because a missed charge signal is worse
than a spurious one, so narrowing it trades one risk for another. The obvious candidates are matching
the header value rather than only its name, excluding `ratelimit` headers explicitly, or requiring a
currency-ish signal — each with different failure modes.

### What the three arms actually are

```
mistral-large-3       WORKS        HTTP 200, usage reported, answered "Ready."
                                   first request ever sent to this provider
gemini-3.8-flash      REACHED      HTTP 503 "This model is currently experiencing high demand.
                                   Spikes in demand are usually temporary. Please try again later."
deepseek-v4.1-flash   UNTESTED     skipped: the false-positive stop ended the probe first
```

**Gemini's 503 is capacity, not credentials.** A 503 with a well-formed API error body means the
request authenticated and reached the model service. Its counting endpoint already answered 33
requests successfully on 2026-09-21. Nothing here suggests a key or billing problem — but it does
mean the arm can be transiently unavailable, and a screen that hits it during a spike will take the
route's error path.

**DeepSeek is still unknown.** The probe stopped before reaching it. I have not re-run: this probe
refuses replay by design, and re-running is a decision rather than a recovery step.

### Money

```
observed spend        $0.000017
held, usage unknown   $0.000314    the Gemini 503 at its full reservation
TOTAL EXPOSURE        $0.000331    of the $0.50 probe allowance
```

Record: `probe-reachability-record.json`. Created exclusively, finalized, no unresolved dispatch, no
resume path. It never read or wrote any screen activation or record.

### What the probe was and was not

One request per arm, 64-token output cap, a fixed one-line prompt. Not a screen, not a comparison,
and not a route to the frozen plan. It ran through the accepted transaction, the accepted egress
capability with the pinned-host allowlist and TLS verification on, and `launch-protocol-v3`, with the
request spec asserted before each dispatch. It did not stage the application, so no product code ran
and no database was opened.

### Where this leaves a continuation

Three things now stand between the current state and a completable screen, and only one of them is
money:

1. **The charge-signal false positive** would stop any run at the first Mistral unit. This is the
   blocker, and it needs a decision on how to narrow the detector.
2. **DeepSeek is untested.** A continuation could still stop there.
3. **Gemini can be transiently unavailable.** Not a blocker, but a source of route errors.

The OpenAI balance, which was the previous blocker, is resolved at $25 and covers even the
pessimistic $23.63 for that arm.

I am not proposing a fix, a re-probe or a continuation. Each is a decision, and after this round I
would rather not guess which one is wanted.

### Codex prompt

Read "Reachability probe" in
`docs/superpowers/2026-09-19-six-model-offline-readiness-handoff.md`. On Jeff's direct authorization I
ran one minimal request per untested arm: $0.000017 observed, $0.000331 exposure. Mistral works and
answered. Gemini is reachable but returned a 503 capacity error. DeepSeek is still untested because

## One batched request — narrow the charge detector, probe DeepSeek, run the continuation

Requested 2026-09-22 at Jeff's direction: batch the remaining work into a single task rather than
three sequential rulings. Nothing below has been built or run. The money is resolved; what is left is
one judgement call and two executions.

### Why one task

Three things stand between here and a completable screen, and they are not independent: the detector
fix has to land before a continuation can finish, and the DeepSeek probe is only worth running as
part of the same pass. Splitting them into three review cycles adds rounds without adding scrutiny —
the whole package is already accepted apart from these.

### 1. The charge-signal detector — the only real judgement call

`detectChargeSignal` flags any response header matching
`/(^|-)(cost|charge|billing|billed)(-|$)/i`. Mistral returns `x-ratelimit-tokens-query-cost` on a
normal 200; it reports tokens counted against the rate limit, not money. A successful Mistral reply
therefore reads as a charge and halts the run.

**The evidence across every record this project holds is one-sided:**

```
legitimate firing   replacement run, gpt-5.6-sol
                    "an error naming billing, payment or exhausted quota"   <- BODY branch
false positive      probe, mistral-large-3
                    "response header x-ratelimit-tokens-query-cost"         <- HEADER branch
```

The branch that has ever been right is the error-body branch. The header branch has fired exactly
once, wrongly. That is a narrow evidence base and I would not over-read it — but it does say the
header test is carrying no demonstrated weight while causing a hard stop.

**What I propose, for your ruling rather than as a decision:** keep every unambiguous signal as a
hard stop, and demote the ambiguous one to a recorded observation.

```
HARD STOP (unchanged)   HTTP 402
                        an error body naming billing, payment or exhausted quota
                        a body or usage field carrying a non-zero cost
RECORDED, NOT A STOP    a header whose NAME matches the cost pattern but which is a rate-limit
                        header, or whose VALUE does not look monetary
```

Nothing is discarded: a demoted header is still retained in the dispatch record and surfaced in the
summary, so a reviewer sees it and a later reading can revisit it.

Alternatives I considered and did not prefer, with their failure modes:

- **Exclude `ratelimit` headers by name only.** Simplest, and fixes this exact case. Fails if another
  provider puts routine telemetry in a differently-named header.
- **Require a monetary-looking value.** Stronger, but a genuine charge header carrying a bare number
  would be missed.
- **Narrow the name pattern to `usd|price|amount|invoice`.** Misses a plain `x-charge`.

The trade is real in both directions: the pattern is broad on purpose, because missing a genuine
billing signal is worse than a spurious stop. I do not want to narrow it on my own judgement, and a
wrong call here is expensive in a way that is hard to detect — a missed signal looks like a run that
simply cost more than expected.

**No offline proof could have caught this.** Every fixture reply carried headers I wrote. A real
provider's header set is exactly what a fixture cannot supply — the same structural blind spot as the
network block. Whatever is decided, the proof for it should include a fixture that replays the
*actual* observed Mistral headers, which the probe record now preserves.

### 2. DeepSeek is still unprobed

The probe stopped before reaching it. One minimal request, 64-token cap, reserves $0.00014 and likely
costs under $0.0003. It is the last arm whose generation endpoint has never been contacted, and it
could stop a continuation exactly as OpenAI did.

prior records are consumed and the launcher refuses a replay at either.

  less replacement run (consumed)     $0.674959

available for the continuation       $69.211960

authority without asserting any of them was invoiced. Provider balances are separate and sufficient —

## Batch results — correction landed, DeepSeek works, screen stopped at 3 of 360 on a second false positive of the same family

Executed 2026-09-22 under "Codex batched authorization - correct, probe DeepSeek, run once." All four

authorized and started. It stopped at 3 of 360 units on **`gpt-5.6-sol: response field billing`**.

**That stop is a false positive of exactly the kind you just ruled on, in the body-field branch
rather than the header branch.** OpenAI's Responses API returns, on every successful response:

```json
"billing": { "payer": "developer" }
```

It declares WHO PAYS - the developer rather than an end user - and carries no amount. The call
succeeded: HTTP 200, `status: "completed"`, a delivered 767-character answer, and settled usage of
45,308 tokens costing $0.230137. `billing` is in `CHARGE_SIGNAL_FIELDS`, the object is truthy, so the
screen halted on a working call.

false positive justifies fixing that false positive, and this is a second observation in a different
branch, so it is yours to rule on rather than mine to generalise from.

A working OpenAI call halts the screen. `billing: {payer: "developer"}` appears on every successful

matches a money word, on a successful response, read as evidence of a charge. Two providers, two
branches, same shape.

provider, mirroring what you ruled for Mistral. The obvious broader move is to require a monetary
VALUE rather than a matching name, which you already rejected for headers, and the same objection
presumably applies here. There may also be a case for distinguishing a field that carries an amount
from one that carries an attribution. That is a judgement about how much generalisation one more
observation licenses, and after being corrected twice on exactly that question I would rather you
made it.

## Codex body-field ruling - payer attribution is metadata; one bounded continuation

Reviewed 2026-09-22T14:40:25.421Z. This is an explicit reassessment and new bounded task under Jeff's
standing delegation to approve sensible fixes inside the approved comparison. The preceding batch
was consumed; this is not permission to restart its identity or an automatic correction allowance.

### Ruling and accepted evidence

**The body-field stop is a false positive. Approve a provider-bound, shape-checked attribution
classification, then one fresh full screen after the checks below pass.** No new owner budget
approval or extra provider probe is required. The original approved outcome, cases and limits stay
fixed, and the conservative remaining allowance is **$68.574341**.

The retained OpenAI response is HTTP 200, status completed, error null, with exactly
`billing: {payer: "developer"}`. Its retained bytes match its original-response digest: no truncation
or redaction accounts for the missing monetary amount. The current detector reports only
`response field billing`; removing just that object removes the signal. This is attribution of the
payer, not evidence of a charge amount. Reported usage still costs $0.230137 under the accepted rates
and must remain fully accounted for. Metadata classification does not mean the generation was free.

I own the earlier instruction to preserve this branch unchanged. A truthy object carrying a billing
name was not a sufficient monetary test. The lesson is to distinguish a recognized metadata shape
from monetary evidence, while keeping unrecognized forms conservative; it is not to remove the
billing field wholesale or require a currency symbol before stopping.

Independent saved-evidence review: **6/6 checks, 23 artifact identities unchanged**. Reproduce with:

`node audit/model-comparison-probe-review-2026-09-22/body-field-review.cjs`

Receipt: `audit/model-comparison-probe-review-2026-09-22/body-field-review.json`. This review made no
provider call, loaded no credential and ran no launcher. It confirms the DeepSeek probe's single
HTTP 200 and $0.000009 usage cost; the screen's eight closed dispatches (five generations, three
counts), three delivered GC-002 first-repeat answers, and incomplete 3/360 disposition. The screen
used $0.637610; the five consumed operations total $1.425659 used or held, leaving $68.574341.
These remain usage-based estimates and conservative holds, not reconciled provider invoices.

The submitted 10/0 gate receipt is preserved and accepted as pre-run evidence. Its executable now
intentionally fails an assertion that the DeepSeek record does not exist, so do not rerun it as an
inactive-state proof or rewrite that assertion. Its classifier cases directly call the helper and
pass the result into the real transaction; they do not themselves send saved response bytes through
the protocol. The actual paid record establishes the OpenAI wiring. The changed path below gets a
focused protocol replay, not a repeat certification of the accepted transport or activation design.

### One correction, with explicit boundaries

1. Version the harness classifier and the minimum wiring needed. Recognize the top-level billing
   object as payer-attribution metadata only for the pinned OpenAI Responses generation request,
   with an ordinary object whose **only own key is payer and whose value is exactly developer**.
   Bind the provider/channel to the request configuration, never to the response's model or claims.
   Do not globally ignore billing, all objects, or all successful responses. This rule does not
   extend to a counting reply, another provider, a different payer, an array, a nested usage field,
   or an object with extra fields. Those remain under the existing conservative stop behavior.
2. Evaluate every independent signal even when attribution metadata is present. HTTP 402, payment/
   exhausted-account errors, numeric monetary headers, explicit body or usage charges, and an
   attribution object with an added amount/unknown key still stop. No currency symbol is required.
   A 200 response can still contain a stopping signal. Keep the accepted Mistral quota exception,
   both-lane stop, reservation, settlement, deadline and unknown-usage behavior unchanged.
3. Retain the sanitized, bounded classification basis and the observed body needed to recompute it.
   Call recognized payer-only content metadata, not zero cost. An unrecognized billing shape may
   still conservatively halt; describe that as unrecognized billing evidence, not a proven charge.
   No general schema framework, recursive money-name scanner, rate change or application edit.

Use the saved OpenAI response, the retained exhausted-credit response, and the already-retained
successful provider generation replies as a small regression corpus. Inventory the available
provider/channel shapes explicitly; absent successful Gemini generation evidence remains absent.

## Screen result — 130 of 360 units, repeat 1 complete across all six arms, stopped on a genuine Google free-tier cap

Executed 2026-09-22 under "Codex body-field ruling - payer attribution is metadata; one bounded
continuation." All three authorized steps ran in order: the payer-attribution classification, the
replay gate against retained bytes, and one fresh 360-unit screen at $68.574341. The screen ran
**19 minutes 3 seconds** and stopped at 130 of 360 units on
**`gemini-3.8-flash: an error naming billing, payment or exhausted quota`**.

I have not repaired anything, retried, restarted, or changed a cap. This is the single consolidated
result.

### The stop is real. It is not a third false positive

The two previous stops were routine metadata read as a charge. This one is not. The retained,
sanitized body:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": 429,
    "message": "You exceeded your current quota, please check your plan and billing details. ...
       * Quota exceeded for metric:
         generativelanguage.googleapis.com/generate_content_free_tier_requests,
         limit: 20, model: gemini-3.8-flash
       Please retry in 1.549823416s.",
    "status": "RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED"
  }
}
```

The metric Google names is `generate_content_free_tier_requests`. **The Gemini key is on the free
tier**, with a 20-request cap. The classifier fired correctly on a real `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, and I
am not proposing a change to it.

One distinction I want to keep straight rather than blur: this is an exhausted **allocation**, not an
unpaid bill. Nothing was charged. Gemini's observed spend is $0.000000 because every one of its calls
failed.

### Gemini never worked at all, from its first call

```
gemini dispatches   22        HTTP 200: 0
                              HTTP 503: 21   "This model is currently experiencing high demand"  UNAVAILABLE
                              HTTP 429:  1   free-tier request cap
first call          14:58:10Z  (seq 11, ~75 seconds into the run)   already 503
last call           15:15:56Z  (seq 251)                            429, run stops
```

Mid-run I flagged Gemini's $0.00 spend as something to watch rather than assume. That was the
symptom: it had failed on every call from the start. The 503 `UNAVAILABLE` responses are consistent
with free-tier capacity rationing, but I can only say *consistent with* — the 429 is the one that
names the free tier outright, and I cannot prove the 503s share that cause without a call that
succeeds on a paid tier.

**The owner has since added $25 to the Google account.** That does not appear in any figure below,
and it does not change this run. It also does not by itself move the key to the paid tier: a
generativelanguage key stays on `free_tier_requests` until billing is enabled on the Google Cloud
project the key belongs to. Whether that is now true is unverified — **I made no Gemini call to check
it, because this task's authorization for provider calls is consumed.**

**A correction to a number a casual reader would take from the record.** The export counts 130
answers, and a naive per-arm count credits Gemini with 11. Those 11 are the application's own string,

The aggregate verdict counts in the record are distorted for the same reason: Gemini's 22 dead units
land in `route-failed` and `limitation-failed` and make the failure categories look worse than the
five working arms did. The verdicts are diagnostic evidence in their own file, not an adjudication,
and they should not be read as a per-arm quality signal in this run.

### Adversarial self-review

**"You called two stops false positives and this one real. What makes this different, other than
convenience?"** The two earlier stops were on HTTP 200 responses that delivered answers and settled
usage; the metadata named money but described payer identity and rate-limit consumption. This is HTTP
429 with `status: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` and a named exhausted quota metric, on a call that delivered
nothing. The difference is in the response, not in what I wanted it to be. If a future stop looks
like this one, it should stop the run too.

**"Is `free tier` really established, or inferred from a message that also says `billing details`?"**
Established. `generate_content_free_tier_requests` is the metric Google itself names. The
`billing details` phrasing is Google's generic advice text and I am not leaning on it.

**"You blamed the 503s on the free tier."** I did not, and I checked this line specifically. The 503
bodies say only `UNAVAILABLE` / high demand. I wrote *consistent with* and I am not upgrading it.

**"106 real answers — did you verify, or subtract what looked wrong?"** Verified by excluding units
whose narrative contains the application's error string, then reading three of them to confirm the
string is the app's and not a model's. A count of 130 is what the export reports; 106 is what I can
defend.

**"Your leak scan flagged `sol` and you dismissed it."** It matched inside `resolved`. That is the
substring-grep failure I have been corrected on before, this time in my own ad-hoc check rather than
in shipped code. The word-boundary scan is the one I am reporting, and the export's built-in scan is
an independent backstop.

**"$4.61 for 130 units projects to about $12.80 for 360."** It does, and I am not presenting that as
a forecast. Sonnet and Sol dominate the spend, retries are uneven across cases, and Gemini contributed
$0 while failing. A completed screen would cost more than a third-of-a-screen extrapolation suggests.

**"The owner added $25. Why not just run again?"** Because the ruling says a material failure ends
this task and no automatic restart follows, and because the launcher refuses a second run at this
identity by design. A continuation needs a fresh activation, which is your call and Jeff's, not a
recovery step I take.

**"Does the $25 fix it?"** Unverified and I did not test it. It addresses the cap only if billing is
enabled on the key's Google Cloud project. A one-call Gemini probe would settle it for well under a
cent, and that is a decision for you rather than something I do because it is cheap.

### What I did not do

No classifier repair. No retry of the stopped unit. No second screen, no fresh activation, no cap
change, no arm removal, no cleanup, no Gemini probe after the credits were added. No source, product,
deployment or commit changes. The record is preserved and finalized.

## The authorized screen was killed by session teardown at 22 of 360 — cause found and fixed, sixth attempt not taken

Executed 2026-09-22 under "Codex screen-result ruling - verify Gemini readiness; preserve the
five-arm diagnostic evidence." Both prerequisites passed and the authorized screen started. It
reached 22 of 360 units and its process died when the agent session that launched it ended.

**It did not stop on a gate, a provider, a classifier or the budget.** No refusal, no charge signal,
no deadline. The record was simply never closed.

### What the probe established first

```
identity matched   true    the exact GC-002 request that failed, byte for byte, hash ea540b94…
count reused       true    49,794 tokens, exact-identity, no counting call made
HTTP 200           2,431 ms
usage              49,794 in / 269 out, priceable
answer             824 characters carrying SQL
dispatches         1 permitted, 1 made; the route's second call was refused by the one-shot bound
observed           $0.038354      held $0
record             probe-record-gemini-readiness-2026-09-22.json
```

The account prerequisite was satisfied by the owner's in-session report of the displayed limits for
the project owning the installed key: **10,000 requests/day, 1,000/minute, 1,000,000 tokens/minute**,
against the 240/day this screen needs and the 20/day free-tier allocation that stopped the fourth
screen. Those figures are recorded in the probe as owner-reported evidence, not as an inspection.

A successful probe establishes that this request worked. It does not explain the 21 earlier 503s and
I am not claiming it does.

### What the screen did before it was killed

```
run id        six-model-screen-8a2bc6529b9181f0
state         in-progress, NEVER FINALIZED
units         22 of 360     dispatches 54, 53 closed, 1 UNRESOLVED
opened        16:00:36Z     last write 16:04:56Z
```

All six arms were answering, Gemini included — the thing four previous attempts never achieved:

```
haiku 7/7 200    sonnet 10/10 200    sol 7/7 200
gemini 4/4 200   mistral 4/4 200     deepseek 3/3 200
```

Money, reconstructed by the accepted reader from durable entries:

```
generation, usage reported     $0.636192
generation, usage unknown      $0.000000
counting, unpriced scenario    $0.310000
outstanding reservations       $0.010628   dispatch #54, mistral GC-021, left in flight
                               ---------
TOTAL POSSIBLE                 $0.956820   of a $63.921937 allowance
```

Cumulative across all eight operations: **$7.034883 used or held, $62.965117 remaining** of the $70.

### The cause, and the fix

The screen ran as a child of the shell inside the agent session. When the session ended, the process
tree went with it. A run that needs roughly 75 minutes cannot live there, and this would have
happened on every attempt regardless of budget, provider or classifier.

`run-detached.ps1` starts the launcher through `Start-Process`, which is not parented to the calling
shell. **Verified rather than asserted**: a dummy writing every two seconds was started this way, the
starting shell exited, and a later separate shell found the file still growing and the process alive.
Had it still been a child, that check reads zero — the failing case and the passing case are
distinguishable. The dummy was stopped and removed.

### What is staged, and what I did not do

```

launch-prep-v10.cjs      10/11 checks pass; the one FAIL is the spending request, which --write creates
identity                 six-model-screen-8a6dbc063a170698   (distinct from all five consumed)

The killed record has no finalized money summary, because nothing closed it. Rather than weaken that
check or write a second accounting method, the prep now rebuilds its exposure from the durable
dispatch entries **using the reader's own `reconstruct` function** — two implementations that can
disagree about money is the defect, not the remedy.

**I did not write the spending request, create an activation, or start a sixth screen.** The ruling
authorized one fresh screen; that screen was launched and was killed by infrastructure rather than by
any condition the ruling contemplated. Whether a relaunch is the same authorization resumed or a new
attempt is a judgement for the reviewer and the owner, not a recovery step I take on my own. No
consumed identity was reactivated and no record was altered.

### Adversarial self-review

**"You lost the run. Did you also lose evidence?"** No. The record is intact and self-describing: the
reader reports `NEVER FINALIZED`, names the one unresolved dispatch and its held amount, and refuses
to compute a disposition. Nothing is inferred to paper over the gap.

**"Is $0.956820 real, or a number you assembled to look tidy?"** It is reconstructed from durable
dispatch entries by the accepted reader, and it includes a $0.010628 hold for a dispatch that was
in flight when the process died and whose outcome is genuinely unknown. That hold is conservative and
is not a claim that the money was billed.

**"22 units across six arms — can anything be said about quality?"** No, and I am not saying it. One
partial repeat, and the ruling bars a ranking from an incomplete screen regardless.

**"You changed the credential path mid-task. Was that in scope?"** It was necessary to run the
authorized screen at all: the keys lived in shell state that does not survive between commands, so
each attempt depended on invisible setup. The loader reads files, reports presence as booleans, and
has no path that returns a value. It touches no product code. The same applies to `run-detached.ps1`.

**"Your first key-shape guard silently refused the real key."** It knew only Google's legacy `AIza`
format; the installed key is the current `AQ.` format. That guard exists to stop a mispaired key
being sent to the wrong provider, so it now names both Google formats explicitly rather than being
loosened to accept anything. I found it by testing the value's shape, never by printing it.

**"Could the detachment fix be wishful?"** It was tested with a case that could fail and did not.
What it does not prove is that a 75-minute run survives a machine reboot or a Windows update, which
is a different exposure and is not addressed here.

## Codex explanation - no returned SQL is several different outcomes

Read-only diagnosis 2026-09-22T17:26:35.892Z, answering Jeff's question about the many apparent SQL failures.
This does not change the Gemini readiness/conditional-run authorization, introduce another launch
gate, or authorize product repairs. Receipt: `audit/model-comparison-probe-review-2026-09-22/no-sql-diagnostic.json`.

The five non-Gemini arms' first repeat has 100 attempted slots. Thirty outcomes include SQL and
seventy do not. **At least 22 of those seventy have SQL in a retained model reply**, including
retries, even though the final delivered outcome contains none. Therefore ?no SQL returned? is not
the same as ?the model failed to write SQL,? and neither establishes which statements executed.
Thirteen of the thirty outcomes with SQL report zero rows; that is another distinct outcome, not
proof that no query was generated. These are selected diagnostic/control cases on synthetic data,
not an estimate of the normal application's success rate.

The saved evidence shows several causes:

- **A shared fallback hides specific explanations.** For GC-047 (nationwide violent crime from 1930
  onward, sent to Current Trends), the retained Haiku, Sol and DeepSeek replies explicitly return
  null SQL and direct the user to Historical Library. The delivered response instead says it could
  not generate a query and asks for a restatement. The frozen Current route's no-SQL branch replaces
  the model explanation using selectNoSqlRefusal; that selector retains the generic template for
  requests outside its established limitation families. The inspected route and refusal-safety
  files match the frozen candidate hashes. This proves lost explanation, not permission to trust
  every unverified model explanation or proof that all desired historical coverage exists.
- **Some no-query answers are intentional.** GC-006 asks for conviction rates, a control-refusal
  request. The models distinguish reported crime from court outcomes. Demographic rate requests
  also encounter missing-denominator restrictions. These should be assessed against their expected
  limitations, rather than counted automatically as failures to produce SQL.
- **Some generated queries are withheld by the application.** GC-032 retained replies contain
  offender-share SQL, yet the final outcome is post-model-validation with no SQL. The question asks
  about a share of crimes, which is not automatically the same as a share of offender records. The
  saved sequence establishes generation followed by validation refusal; it does not certify every
  rejection as correct or incorrect. Other structural/semantic refusals need their own trace.
- **Some behavior does differ by model.** For GC-051, ?what months does 2026 include??, Haiku's saved
  reply answers in prose and says no SQL is needed. Sol and DeepSeek instead supply SQL. The app's
  generic no-SQL response obscures Haiku's original reasoning. This is a concrete difference to
  assess, not a five-model ranking or proof that the prose answer is sufficiently grounded.
- **Service failure is separate.** Gemini generated no usable response in this run. Mistral GC-021
  also hit a service error, and Sonnet GC-087 ended in an application error. Those must not be
  diagnosed simply as inability to write SQL.

The practical implication is that a model change alone cannot remove the shared fallback behavior.
The existing offline diagnostic assessment should separate supported-query failures, appropriate
limitations, source routing/explanation losses, rejected SQL, execution/empty-result outcomes, and
service/application errors before recommending a repair. Preserve the candidate during comparison.
Neither forcing SQL for every question nor bypassing validation is an authorized remedy.

### Short Claude prompt

Read ?Codex explanation - no returned SQL is several different outcomes.? Within the already-authorized offline
diagnostic review, trace missing delivered SQL from retained model replies through validation and
final output. Keep intentional limitations, model omissions, application rejection, source-routing
messages and service errors separate. GC-047 and GC-051 are retained examples; no product repair,
new paid call or change to the Gemini continuation scope is authorized by this explanation.

Claude's saved results contain several distinct causes behind the same generic failure message.
This diagnosis focuses the existing review on the actual causes so a model choice is not mistaken
for a complete product fix.


## Codex request-contract finding - historical cases were sent with the wrong source selector

Recorded 2026-09-22T17:31:41.477Z, while answering Jeff's questions about the high no-SQL rate and whether
the test should primarily contain answerable requests. **Material harness defect confirmed. Hold
further paid comparison launches.** The earlier conditional launch instructions do not override this
new contradiction. The separately submitted session-teardown/detached-launch proposal has not been
reviewed or approved here; this finding must be resolved before any successor comparison activation.
No running process was stopped or changed by this review.

### What is established

The accepted runner `launch-run-v3.cjs` constructs the application request with
`{question, tab: testCase.tab, sessionId, pageToken}`. It sends no `mode`. The frozen
`app/api/query/route.ts` selects Historical only when `body.mode === "historical"`; otherwise it
selects Current. The real chat component sends `mode`. The test does not match that interface.

The result record then copies `testCase.tab` back into its own metadata. Thus a record labelled
Historical is not evidence that the application actually selected Historical. The recorded route
filename cannot distinguish the two sources because they share the same route.

Read-only boundary reconstruction from these exact code snippets confirms:

- `{tab: "historical"}` selects Current.
- The counterfactual `{mode: "historical"}` selects Historical.
- The inspected route hash matches the frozen candidate.
- The retained GC-047 model replies describe Current's 2022-2026 coverage and direct the reader to
  Historical, consistent with the actual selection rather than the fixture label.

Receipt: `audit/model-comparison-probe-review-2026-09-22/source-selector-review.json`. This is source
inspection plus boundary reconstruction and retained-response evidence, not a claimed new full-route
execution. No credentials, provider calls, real database access or product edits were used.

Six frozen cases request Historical: GC-046, GC-067, GC-082, GC-118, GC-047 and GC-006. Their
first-repeat slots number 36 across six arms, including **30 of the 100 non-Gemini slots** previously
described as a matched five-arm cohort. These are affected experimental inputs, not clean evidence
of model ability on Historical. Even a refusal that looks right does not certify source fidelity.
Other cases retain their evidence but have not thereby become independently adjudicated correct.

### Correction to my prior explanation and acceptance

I previously described GC-047 as sent to Current without checking that its frozen fixture intended
Historical. The backend's replacement of the explanation is observable, but the upstream mismatch
is in the test runner. It is not proof that the user-facing Historical selector is broken: the real
chat component sends the field the route expects. I missed this contract mismatch during readiness
review. Transport, spending, classifier and hash checks did not establish that the intended source
was selected, and I should not have treated them as sufficient experiment readiness.

Accordingly, **do not infer that five models cannot write Historical SQL from this run**. Do not use
the affected slots in a quality ranking, automatically mark their refusals as model failures, or
silently drop them and report a better score. Preserve the recorded bytes and flag the affected cases
consistently across arms and attempts using this runner. The earlier permission for blinded
diagnostic reading remains, with these slots identified as experiment defects rather than model
quality evidence. No formal winner selection was authorized and none is justified.

### The test-design question

The frozen twenty contain **13 required answers, one answer-or-clarification, and six required
refusals**. Thus 65% strictly require an answer, 5% allow clarification, and 30% require refusal.
That is a targeted diagnostic/control screen, not a representative test of ordinary user success.
A required answer must be grounded in supplied data; SQL existing is only an intermediate condition.
A verified metadata answer may also be useful without a fresh query.

For a future ordinary-use acceptance set, my recommendation is roughly **80-90% demonstrated
answerable requests** and 10-20% refusal/clarification controls, with results reported separately.
That is a recommendation, not a retroactive change to this frozen experiment or an authorization to
add paid cases. First establish that the intended source, schema, rows, request fields and expected
answer agree. An otherwise adequate model cannot compensate for being tested against the wrong
dataset. Keep a correct-refusal score separate from useful-answer success.

### One bounded offline task for Claude

Under Jeff's standing delegation for sensible fixes, authorize **one harness-only request-contract
correction and consolidated offline submission**. Preserve product files and all consumed evidence.
Match the real application's request interface for every frozen source, including conversation
history where the frozen case requires it. Verify source selection inside the staged route and
at the constructed model request, not from the runner's copied label.

Carry a decisive old-runner/fixed-runner witness for a Historical case and a Current control through
the actual staged route using offline model replies and disposable fixtures. Use distinct fixture
values/sentinels so Current and Historical cannot accidentally pass the same expected result. Check
all twenty cases for intended source and required request fields; preserve the established separate
NIBRS/SHR route behavior. Record the affected native request identities, prompt/count changes and
which prior measurements remain valid; never transfer an old count onto a changed native body.
Do not silently repair the application, rewrite expected answers, select easier cases or change
model settings to mask the failure. Submit one reviewable correction with truthful coverage, impact
on the existing launch package and remaining allowance, and retained evidence hashes.

No paid call, additional counting endpoint request, probe, activation, fresh generation, source
operation, deployment, commit or automatic correction round is authorized by this task. The new
source-selection proof must be reviewed before launch authority is restored. This is a concrete
correctness hold on the experiment, not another request for Jeff to approve the same budget.

### Short Claude prompt

Read ?Codex request-contract finding - historical cases were sent with the wrong source selector.? Hold further paid comparison
launches. The runner sends tab but the frozen Current/Historical route reads mode, so six Historical
cases actually select Current. Complete the one bounded harness-only request-contract correction;
prove actual source selection and delivered behavior offline, inventory affected prompts/counts,
and submit once. Preserve all product code and receipts. No provider call or activation.

Claude's records let us identify a test setup error that made several models appear to fail on the
wrong data source. Correcting and proving that setup comes before spending on another comparison,
so the test can tell us something trustworthy about the models.

### The correction

`launch-run-v4.cjs`. The v3 body was `{question, tab, sessionId, pageToken}`; `tab` is not part of
the route's interface. The corrected body matches `components/RtciChat.tsx:160`:

```
shared Current/Historical route   { question, history, mode, sessionId, pageToken }
nibrs and shr routes              { question, history, sessionId, pageToken }
```

`mode` is sent only where a mode exists. NIBRS and SHR are separate routes that select by route
identity and read no `mode`, so sending them one would be inventing an interface they do not have.
`history` is now sent everywhere because all three routes read `body.history` and the real client
sends it; all twenty frozen cases carry `history: []`, so this changes no prompt — measured below
rather than assumed.

`launch-run-v3.cjs` is untouched at `722608a09a42a796`. v4 is a new file.

### The witness: 9 of 9, and the old lane has to fail

`00c5a320c0d219c71df9b0852c66987b623582321c04171edc47704811078992`

Through the actual staged route, with a local stub model and disposable fixtures:

```

new contract, historical case   mode=historical    model saw HISTORICAL    expected historical   ok
new contract, current control   mode=current       model saw CURRENT       expected current      ok
```

The observable is the one you named: the system prompt on the constructed model request.
`route.ts:1863` sets `systemPrompt = isHistorical ? getHistoricalSystemPrompt() : undefined` and
`lib/claude.ts:658` puts it on the wire, so the two sources send **demonstrably different bytes**.
The expected Historical prompt is read from the *staged* product at run time and compared by hash,
so Current cannot satisfy the Historical assertion by accident. Three lanes produced two distinct
prompt hashes, and a check asserts that — if they collapsed to one, every other check would be
meaningless and this says so.

The in-route observation point (the source the route records in its own query log) was **not
available** in this staging: no query log is exposed. I report that as not established rather than
claiming two independent confirmations when I have one.

**One of my own defects, found here.** The first run of this witness sent an empty page token, the
route answered 403 before reaching the model, and the old lane recorded "no model call" — which
looks like a failure to select Current but is really a failure to get through the door. A lane that
never reaches the model proves nothing about source selection. The token is now minted properly and
a check requires every lane to have reached the model.

## Nine-case cause table — the product discards usable SQL more often than the models fail to write it

Executed 2026-09-22 under "Codex contract-correction ruling." Offline throughout: retained response
bytes, the staged product's own guardrail and scorer, disposable fixture databases. No provider call,
credential, counting request, product edit, activation or allowance use. All four of your
corrections to my previous reading are accepted and carried below.

### The selection, written before anything was read

`diagnose-selection.cjs` / `diagnose-selection.json`. The rule is fixed in code and mentions nothing
about what any unit contains: the nine cases in your order, each case's eighteen units sorted by
(repeat, then frozen arm order), the **first** non-`answer-correct` unit as the failing trace and the
**first** `answer-correct` unit as the control. For an answer-required case only `answer-correct`
counts as a pass — a stated limitation did not answer a question it was required to answer.

**13 traces** (nine failing, four controls), inside the eighteen cap. Five cases have no successful
unit anywhere in eighteen attempts: GC-032, GC-065, GC-097, GC-080, GC-087.

### The cause table

```
case     arm          k  calls  model SQL  delivered  verdict         cause
GC-032   haiku        F    2    yes        no         answer-wrong    product-rejection-or-error
GC-065   haiku        F    2    yes        no         answer-wrong    product-rejection-or-error
GC-097   haiku        F    2    yes        no         answer-wrong    product-rejection-or-error
GC-061   sol          F    2    yes        no         answer-wrong    product-rejection-or-error
GC-021   haiku        F    2    yes        yes        answer-wrong    model-omission-or-wrong-sql
GC-051   haiku        F    1    no         no         answer-wrong    model-omission-or-wrong-sql
GC-080   haiku        F    2    yes        yes        answer-wrong    unknown
GC-002   haiku        F    2    yes        yes        answer-wrong    unknown
GC-087   haiku        F    2    yes        yes        answer-wrong    unknown
GC-051   sol          C    2    yes        yes        answer-correct  control-passed
GC-002   haiku        C    2    yes        yes        answer-correct  control-passed
GC-021   sonnet       C    2    yes        yes        answer-correct  control-passed
GC-061   haiku        C    1    yes        yes        answer-correct  control-passed
```

`product-rejection-or-error` 4 · `model-omission-or-wrong-sql` 2 · `unknown` 3 · `control-passed` 4.

**In eight of nine failing traces the model produced SQL.** Only GC-051/haiku produced none.

### Product rejection is two different mechanisms, not one

**One is a guardrail false positive.** GC-032/haiku wrote 620 characters of SQL against the right
table with the right filters. `findNibrsSqlIssues` — the product's own function, run here on the
retained SQL — fires `nibrs-undeclared-table-alias`:

```
"Your SQL references undeclared table alias(es): t."
   ... FROM youth_offenders y, total_offenders t
```

`t` **is** declared. Isolated on minimal statements through the same function:

```
FROM t1 a, t2 b              FIRES     <- comma join, both aliases declared
FROM t1 a JOIN t2 b ON ...   clean     <- same query, explicit JOIN
SELECT a.x, zz.y FROM t1 a   FIRES     <- genuinely undeclared; the rule still works
```

The rule does not recognize comma-separated FROM items. The request then declined at
`app/api/nibrs-query/route.ts:1349`, and the retry prompt pushed the model into `sql: null` plus a
demographic-denominator refusal — the exact refusal this case's frozen obligation forbids. The
product rejected a good query and then taught the model to decline.

**The other, and the larger one, is the query contract validator.** GC-065, GC-097 and GC-061 all
declined at `lib/query-contract-validator.ts:26`, and their SQL is **clean** under the NIBRS
guardrails. GC-065's retry produced 1,618 characters of guardrail-clean SQL and was still refused.
Three of the four product rejections are this layer, and the record does not retain which of its
rules fired.

### GC-021, which you flagged — and a hypothesis of mine that was wrong

You asked for the delivered table, prose and fixture result together. I have them, because this is
the one trace whose SQL survived the record intact.

My first hypothesis was that the scorer was discriminating on surface form: haiku wrote "Ward, AR"
and sonnet wrote "Ward, Arkansas". **That was wrong.** Feeding both narratives the same rows makes
both fail, so the wording is not what separates them. The difference is the SQL:

```
haiku    SELECT SUM(count) AS murders ...                    -> [{"murders":20}]
sonnet   SELECT year, agency, state, SUM(count) AS murders
           ... GROUP BY year, agency, state ...              -> (bindings included)
```

Re-executing haiku's SQL on the staged fixture returns exactly `{"murders": 20}` — the right number —
and re-running the scorer on it **reproduces the recorded `answer-wrong` exactly**, with the reason
`a claim of 20 names no entity, not Ward`. Neither narrative states the figure, so the only place the
value could be bound to Ward/2022 is the table, and haiku's query returned a bare scalar.

**The scorer is behaving correctly here.** An unlabeled "20" is precisely what a crime-data product
should not present as an answer. This is a real difference in what the two queries selected, not an
evaluator artifact, and I withdraw the surface-form hypothesis.

I cannot re-score sonnet's control the same way: its SQL is truncated in the record, so its re-score
is not evidence and is not offered as any.

### Why three traces stay unknown — and it is a recording limit, not an analysis gap

**The record caps `sqlDelivered` at exactly 200 characters.** Every trace that would not execute is
exactly 200 long and is a strict prefix of the model's own retained SQL. GC-021's failing trace is
137 characters, which is the only reason it could be settled at all.

So GC-080, GC-002 and GC-087 delivered rows, failed, and cannot be reconstructed: the query that
produced the table is cut off in the middle. I mark them `unknown` rather than assume they share
GC-021's mechanism, though the narratives are suggestive — none states a figure, so all three depend
entirely on whether their SQL selected the binding columns.

An earlier version of this tool guessed truncation from SQLite error text and missed the cases whose
cut landed on a plausible-looking identifier. The 200-character cap is exact; the error text is not.

### The five refusal cases, tallied separately and never selected from

```
GC-026   18 limitation-stated                 all pass
GC-009   11 limitation-stated, 7 failed
GC-075   18 limitation-failed                 none pass
GC-096   18 limitation-failed                 none pass
GC-106   18 limitation-failed                 none pass
```

Three refusal cases fail on all eighteen units across all six arms. A failure that uniform across
independent models is more likely an expectation or check problem than six models making the same
mistake — but that is a hypothesis, it was outside this task, and nothing here tests it.

### One recommended next scope

**Instrument the two decline layers and raise the SQL retention cap, then re-read this same record.
No new paid run.**

Concretely, and all in the harness rather than the product:

1. Retain the **full** delivered SQL instead of 200 characters, and retain the delivered rows (or a
   bounded sample). This alone converts the three `unknown` traces, and the same class across the
   whole record, into decidable ones.
2. Retain **which contract rule fired** when `lib/query-contract-validator.ts:26` ends a request.
   Three of four product rejections came from that one line and the record cannot say why.
3. Re-run the trace tool over all 252 unaffected units with those two fields present, to turn these
   thirteen representative traces into an actual prevalence count.

That order matters: today the highest-value unknown is not a model question, it is that the record
cannot say why the product refused. Only after (1) and (2) is it worth deciding between repairing
the comma-join guardrail, revisiting the contract layer, or paying for another comparison.

What I am **not** recommending: no product repair, no change to frozen expectations or scoring rules,
no new test mix, no recount, no further paid run. The comma-join guardrail defect is real and
reproducible but repairing it would change the frozen candidate, which per your ruling I am flagging
rather than doing.

### Adversarial self-review

**"Four causes from thirteen traces is a thin base."** It is, and the traces were chosen by a rule
fixed in advance precisely so the thinness cannot be selective. It is not a prevalence estimate and
the document says so three times.

**"You called a guardrail broken."** I ran the product's own function on the model's own retained SQL
and then isolated the behaviour on minimal statements, including a control that still fires correctly.
The finding is that the rule has a blind spot on comma joins, not that it is broken.

**"You reversed yourself on GC-021."** Yes — the surface-form hypothesis was wrong and I tested it
rather than shipping it. The corrected reading makes the scorer right and the model's query the
problem, which is the less convenient direction.

**"Three unknowns look like giving up."** They are the direct consequence of a 200-character cap that
I located exactly and can name. That is a finding, and it is the first item of the recommendation.

**"Does any of this bear on model choice?"** No, and deliberately none of it is framed that way.
Eight of nine failing traces produced SQL, which is consistent with your correction that "no SQL
returned" is not "no SQL generated". It is not evidence about which model to use.

```

## Codex nine-case ruling - accept the alias defect; reconstruct evidence without inventing causes

Reviewed 2026-09-22T18:47:02.257Z. **Accept the fixed selection, reproduced alias false positive, and recorded
evidence gaps. Do not accept the whole cause table as settled root-cause attribution. Authorize
one bounded harness-only offline reconstruction task, with the feasibility gate below, rather than
claiming that fuller logging can restore fields never saved in the original record.** No paid run,
recount, product repair, frozen-rule change or activation is authorized.

### What reproduces

Independent review **6/6**, with the prior **38 artifact identities unchanged**. The thirteen traces
reproduce on disposable fixtures; the submitted trace receipt was preserved by redirecting its
output to a new reviewer receipt. Selection follows the stated fixed rule; its receipt predates the
trace receipt. Evidence:

- `audit/model-comparison-probe-review-2026-09-22/nine-case-review.json`
- `audit/model-comparison-probe-review-2026-09-22/diagnose-trace-replay.json`
- `audit/model-comparison-probe-review-2026-09-22/diagnose-independent-witnesses.json`

GC-032's comma-join alias rejection is confirmed using the staged guardrail and both controls:
declared comma aliases fail, explicit JOIN aliases pass, and an actually undeclared alias still
fails. Independently executing the retained initial query on the disposable NIBRS fixture returns
**youth_share_pct 8.6, youth_count 1200, total_count 14000**, matching the frozen arithmetic. This is
a concrete product false positive, not merely valid syntax. It does not license bypassing other
checks or changing the frozen candidate during this comparison. Keep it as a named repair candidate.

### Narrow the causal claims

1. **Eight failures produced SQL; only four withheld it.** The other four delivered SQL: GC-021
   and the three still-unknown delivery cases. Correct the progress-page claim that the application
   discarded SQL in all eight. Generated, accepted, executed, delivered and correctly answered are
   separate observations.
2. **The three contract messages locate a rejection family, not a demonstrated product defect.**
   Line 26 defines a shared message constant, not the rule that fired or a unique runtime branch.
   Passing findNibrsSqlIssues is not proof of semantic correctness. For example, GC-065's initial
   guardrail-clean query selects the smallest 2025 total; it does not calculate a decrease between
   periods. Its later retry is a different statement needing its own trace. GC-061 is SHR, and the
   submitted tool does not run the NIBRS guardrail on it at all: its guardrail fields are null. Do not
   label that an observed clean result. Credit the observed product refusals; keep their legitimacy
   and precise causes unresolved until the actual rule/results are observed.
3. **GC-021 reproduces the scorer, not an independent proof that the model's SQL was wrong.**
   The SQL obtains the correct 20 from the supplied data and filters Ward/AR/2022. The accompanying
   narrative explicitly names murders, Ward, AR and 2022. A one-cell table headed murders with that
   accompanying description is not simply an unexplained naked number to a reader. The scorer
   extracts table bindings only from that row, separately from prose; it cannot use this contextual
   association. The same scalar passes if the prose explicitly says "Ward, Arkansas reported 20
   murders in 2022", and the original prose passes if agency/state/year columns are added. These
   controls establish representation-sensitive scoring, not automatic correctness of its policy.
   Keep the original frozen verdict; classify the unresolved issue as delivery/evaluator binding,
   not a settled wrong-SQL defect. Do not change scoring rules or infer missing table context.
4. **GC-051 establishes a model SQL omission, not necessarily false factual content.** The retained
   reply answers in prose and says SQL is unnecessary. Whether those availability facts were
   adequately grounded and whether the application should have delivered them is a separate
   question. A SQL-required experiment can record the omission without conflating it with all forms
   of answering incorrectly.
5. The three truncated-delivery cases correctly remain unknown from the recorded delivery fields.
   Their retention cap is real, but a schema change now cannot recover original rows or final SQL.
   Nor does a prefix of a model query establish the exact post-validation query that executed.

Uniform failures across models are a useful lead, not proof that a scorer/expectation is wrong:
shared product behavior, fixture limitations and shared model mistakes remain alternatives.
No prevalence or model ranking follows from these thirteen selected traces.

### One feasible next task: separate offline replay evidence

**Approve harness-only observation and replay using the existing retained replies.** All **561
original generation responses are retained without truncation or redaction**, and their retained
text digests verify. This makes reconstruction plausible; it does not guarantee all 252 units can
be reconstructed. Preserve original records and their verdicts byte for byte. New evidence must
be clearly labelled reconstructed, with links/hashes to the original unit and dispatches.

The work is one integrated task with an internal gate, not a separate prototype/review cycle:

1. Add observation in versioned harness code only: full delivered SQL, actual delivered columns and
   rows, narrative and relevant presentation context, executed-query observation where available,
   and each contract validation's fired rules/block reasons and the input SQL it evaluated. Observe
   the **frozen staged modules**, including their accepted reversed copies, rather than searching
   today's working-tree message strings. Wrappers must preserve arguments, return values and thrown
   errors. Do not replace a failed decision or modify the product file to make observation easier.
2. Replay the same thirteen selected units first, using the frozen candidate and disposable fixtures
   matching the original manifest. Feed only retained native provider responses through the accepted
   adapters. Match the actual constructed native request identity, provider/arm, case, repeat,
   purpose and dispatch order before releasing each saved reply. Preserve the original request
   semantics for this unaffected cohort; the source correction must not be used to turn a different
   prompt into a purported replay. Match known terminal status, narrative, normalized SQL prefix,
   row count and frozen verdict, and check all saved replies were consumed in the expected order.
   Never claim restored original capture merely because these available fields agree.
3. Install a no-network guard and a refusal on any absent/mismatched/truncated needed response or
   unexpected extra call. No real keys, live fallback, new generation, count endpoint or unbounded
   retry. Existing exact-identity counts/retained count replies may be reused where the replay
   requires them; a missing measurement is a replay limitation, not authority to obtain one.
   Clocks or runtime context that affect request bytes must be reconstructed from recorded evidence
   or reported as divergence, not guessed into a match.
4. Capture the complete delivered table within the existing route row bound and established payload
   limits. A sample alone cannot settle an obligation about omitted rows, totals or membership.
   Any retention overflow must be explicit and leave dependent judgments unknown. The 200-character
   SQL cap must not survive silently in the reconstructed evidence. Preserve full statements and
   distinguish model SQL from transformed/executed SQL; do not substitute one for another.
5. If the thirteen-unit gate demonstrates faithful replay and observational neutrality, continue in
   the same task across **at most the 252 unaffected-by-source units**. Do not replay the 108
   source-affected units as corrected model outcomes. Report every unit in the denominator, including
   replay failures/unknowns; do not select only recoverable units. A failed feasibility gate stops
   expansion and yields one consolidated limitation report, not a new provider operation.
